t: LeetCode 2160 — Minimum Sum of Four Digit Number After Splitting Digits
o: The four digits of num must all be reused to build two integers new1 and new2 (leading zeros allowed, any digit distribution), and we minimize their sum. For num = 2932 the digits 2,2,3,9 can form 29 and 23, and indeed 29 + 23 = 52 is minimal — far better than lopsided splits like 223 + 9 = 232. For num = 4009, leading zeros make the tiny numbers 4 and 9 legal, giving 4 + 9 = 13. Because num has exactly four digits (1000..9999), the whole search space is minuscule; the exercise is recognizing which arrangement wins and why.
k: new1 + new2 = 10*(sum of tens digits) + (sum of units digits): tens places carry ten times the weight.
Therefore the two smallest digits belong in the tens places and the two largest in the units places.
Exactly four digits means every viable strategy runs in O(1); the problem tests reasoning, not speed.

a.n: Approach 1: Enumerate all permutations and splits
a.i: With only four digits there are at most 24 orderings and 3 cut points, so exhaustively forming every (new1, new2) via a permutation plus a split is completely safe. This brute force needs no insight, always succeeds, and neatly validates the greedy formula that follows.
s: Generate all 24 permutations of the digit string.
Cut each permutation at each of the three interior positions.
Parse both parts as integers (leading zeros handled naturally).
a.t: O(1) — 24 permutations times 3 cut points on 4 fixed digits

a.n: Approach 2: Sort digits and balance the tens places (optimal)
a.i: Writing new1 = 10*a + c and new2 = 10*b + d shows the sum is 10*(a+b) + c + d: tens digits weigh ten times more than units digits. Sorted digits d0 <= d1 <= d2 <= d3 should therefore place d0 and d1 in the tens positions and d2, d3 in the units positions — exactly the pairing behind 29 + 23 = 52 for 2932 and 4 + 9 = 13 for 4009.
s: Extract the four digits and sort ascending.
Put the two smallest digits in the tens places, the two largest in the units places.

w: Mention the 24-permutation brute force first, then present the weighted-digit argument — that progression demonstrates structured thinking. Pitfalls: misassigning WHICH two digits get the tens places (they are the two smallest), forgetting leading zeros are permitted (4009 resolves via 4 + 9 precisely because of that), and building numbers with unequal digit counts when balanced two-digit pairs are always at least as good. Follow-ups: split into k numbers, minimize the product new1*new2, or maximize the sum.
